cards.explanation: The answer is righteous judgment. Moses says the judges are to judge the people "…with righteous judgment." Not fast judgment, not popular judgment, righteous. A judge who rules on mood is just a person with a hunch and a nice chair.

The answer is that a bribe blinds their eyes and twists their words. Moses says "…a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous." Notice who he's talking about, friends: the wise and the righteous. If it can get to them, nobody should think they're too sharp for it.

The answer is land. Moses says to pursue justice so that they may live and possess the land the LORD their God is giving them. Notice it says giving, friends. It's a gift they're walking into. And justice, and justice alone, is how they're to live in it.

The answer is a sacred pillar. Moses says, "…do not set up for yourselves a sacred pillar, which the LORD your God hates." That's a strong word, and it's right there in the verse. It sits right beside the Asherah pole, so he's closing the door on both.

The answer is True. Moses says not to sacrifice to the LORD an ox or a sheep "…with any defect or serious flaw…" He calls that detestable to the LORD your God. The offering is supposed to be a good one, friends.
The answer is to investigate it thoroughly. Moses says, "…you must investigate it thoroughly." A report is only a report until somebody checks. And thoroughly means all the way, not a quick peek.

The answer is two or three witnesses. Moses says, "On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death…" This is a heavy part, friends, and the rule is careful for a reason I think we can feel. One voice alone is never enough.

The answer is the place the LORD will choose. Moses says, "…you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose." Notice he doesn't name the place yet. The LORD does the choosing, and the people do the going.
The answer is priests. Moses says to go "…to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time." Both of them together, priests and judge, friends. That's who gives the verdict.

The answer is False. Moses says, "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you." That leaves no room for a little adjustment. You don't get to edit the verdict because you'd have written it differently.

The answer is that he must be put to death, and I'll say it plain: this one is heavy. Moses says the man who acts presumptuously and refuses to listen to the priest or the judge "…must be put to death." He adds, "You must purge the evil from Israel." It's a serious thing to refuse the verdict.

The answer is True. Moses says, "Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly." The whole people hear about it, and it shapes how they act. Verse 13 is easy to skim past when the verses right before it are so heavy, friends. I'd say it's worth slowing down for.

The answer is the LORD their God. Moses says, "…you are to appoint over yourselves the king whom the LORD your God shall choose." Israel does the appointing, but the choosing belongs to the LORD. Even the king is picked by Him.

The answer is False. Moses says, "Appoint a king from among your brothers; you are not to set over yourselves a foreigner who is not one of your brothers." No strong leader exception is in there, friends. The line is drawn plainly.

The answer is that the LORD said never to go back that way. Moses says, "…for the LORD has said, ‘You are never to go back that way again.’" The king must not acquire many horses for himself, and he must not send the people back to Egypt to get more. The reason Moses gives for that second part is what the LORD said.
The answer is heart. Moses says the king must not take many wives for himself, "…lest his heart go astray." It's the heart he's watching over, friends. Not the throne and not the treasury.

The answer is False. Moses says the king "…must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold." He's got a list of things the king can't stack up: horses, wives, and now silver and gold. That's a king who has to hold things loosely.

The answer is all the days of his life. The scroll "…is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life…" Not a one-time read and then onto the shelf, friends. Every day for as long as he lives.

The answer is fear. Moses says the king reads "…so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes." Reading and keeping the words go together. That's how the learning happens.

The answer is True. The king is to write himself a copy of the instruction and read from it all the days of his life, "…so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes." (Deuteronomy 17:19). Then Moses says, "…his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen…" (Deuteronomy 17:20). So the scroll isn't just for owning, friends, it's for learning and observing. A king who copies it by hand and keeps coming back to it? That's a king getting his heart humbled one page at a time.

The answer is that he and his sons reign many years. Moses says it's "…in order that he and his sons may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel." Notice his sons are in there too, friends. Keeping the instruction touches more than just the king.
